newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Iranian leader arrives in Tajikistan.
newsitem.headline: Iranian leader arrives in Tajikistan.

text.p: Iranian President Ali Akbar Rafsanjani arrived on Friday in war-ravaged Tajikistan but a planned meeting of Tajik, Afghan and Iranian leaders looked likely to be postponed until Saturday.

Rafsanjani passed through crowds of enthusiastic schoolchildren and students cheering him with Iranian and Tajik flags and portraits of Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov. The two neighbouring states have historic ties and are also linked by language.
Foreign leaders are rare visitors in this remote, ex-Soviet republic bordering China and Afghanistan and ravaged by a four-year civil war.
"(Rafsanjani) and Rakhmonov are likely to discuss issues of bilateral relations and the way to a peaceful settlement in Tajikistan," Zafar Saidov, spokesman to the Tajik president, told Reuters.
Saidov said that Rakhmonov and Rafsanjani were expected to meet later on Friday and sign a set of documents but he gave no details.

A source from Tajikistan's foreign ministry said the meeting of Rakhmonov, Rafsanjani and ousted Afghan President Burhanuddin Rabbani -- scheduled initially for May 9 -- was being postponed due to a delay in Rabbani's own arrival.

The three presidents had been due to discuss regional security and the Afghan war on Friday but Rabbani -- driven out of the Afghan capital Kabul by the purist Islamic Taleban militia last September -- has postponed his arrival in Tajikistan until May 10.

Tajikistan, like Central Asia's other ex-Soviet republics, is concerned that the Taleban may launch a summer offensive to gain control of northern Afghan territory controlled by the anti-Taleban forces of General Abdul Rashid Dostum and commander Ahmad Shah Masood.
Rakhmonov aired worries recently that up to a million refugees could flood his war-wracked country from northern Afghanistan if hostilities restarted.
Iran, itself an Islamist republic, has repeatedly criticised Afghan's Taleban for its extremist interpretations of Islam.
Last December, Rakhmonov's secular government and the country's armed Islamist opposition agreed to a ceasefire after four years of civil war.
But the fragile peace is often disturbed by armed maverick bands and drug traders operating out of bases in Afghanistan.
